SO, WHERE ARE ALL THESE INVESTORS COMING FROM?

There is a curious habit in Nigerian politics: when the economy is struggling, every bad number is presented as proof that Nigeria is collapsing but when investors begin putting money into the country, suddenly those investors become invisible.

That argument does not survive contact with the evidence.

The International Monetary Fund has repeatedly acknowledged that President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s administration undertook major reforms including the removal of fuel subsidies, improvement of the foreign-exchange market, ending monetary financing of the fiscal deficit and strengthening revenue mobilisation.

The IMF’s 2025 assessment was particularly clear: the reforms had improved macroeconomic stability and resilience, strengthened investor confidence, helped Nigeria return to international capital markets and contributed to the resumption of portfolio inflows.

The World Bank has unequivocally said the same thing as the IMF.

In its Nigeria Development Update, the World Bank said reforms since May 2023 were beginning to restore macroeconomic stability, improve fiscal health and rebuild foreign-exchange reserves. It specifically argued that staying the course with the reforms would help promote investment, growth and job creation. 

The World Bank Group says that in fiscal year 2026 it is helping mobilise up to $5.79 billion in private financing for Nigeria, using investment platforms, risk mitigation and commercial financing. The Bank explicitly connects this effort to reforms in foreign exchange management, public finances, fuel subsidies and the investment environment. 

So when somebody says investors have lost confidence in Nigeria, the obvious question is:

Then who exactly is putting all this money into the country?

For instance, China Overseas Engineering Corporation (COVEC) invested $350 million in Katsina and Jigawa, covering agricultural infrastructure, maize cultivation, fisheries, leather processing and renewable energy.

In the same vein and region, Diamond New Energy in July 2026 (just few months back), built and commissioned $250 million lithium processing plant in Nasarawa (the largest in Africa), in collaboration with Jiuling and Canmax. The facility has the processing capacity of 6,000 tonnes of lithium per day. 

Furthermore, Coca-Cola announced plans in September 2024 to invest $1 billion in Nigeria over five years. It is worthy of noted that Coca-Cola company has already invested approximately $1.5 billion in Nigeria.

Similarly, dear political junketing Peter, APM Terminals reaffirmed a $500 million investment commitment to expand their Nigerian operations, particularly around sea ports infrastructure and logistics. 

Just in case your dementia has gotten worse, the Inner Galaxy Steel from China committed about $300 million to establish a specialized steel production plant in Ogun State. As a matter of fact, the Federal Ministry of Steel Development explicitly described the investment as evidence of confidence in Nigeria’s direction under the Renewed Hope Agenda. 

In 2025, Visa also stated it had already made more than $1 billion in investments in Nigeria, including a $200 million investment in Interswitch, while also pursuing plans for a Nigerian data centre.

May I remind your bland memory that the International Finance Corporation/Lagos Free Zone committed up to $50 million in equity to Lagos Free Zone to support expansion of Nigeria’s private deep-sea-port-based special economic zone. The zone itself openly stated that it has attracted approximately $2.75 billion in investment from different parts of the world.

Additionally, JBS (the Brazilian meat giant) record shows a $2.5 billion investment proposal in Nigeria for four to five years following a letter of intent. 

Likewise, the Nigeria-South Africa investment engagement also announced the potential investment of approximately R117.7 billion in Nigeria over the period of three to five years.

Burgum is pushing another federal land swap at Cumberland Island National Seashore in Georgia, just like the one at Yosemite.

Both use the same move: hand federal park land to private interests, funded in part by the Land and Water Conservation Fund, money meant for conservation.

Two wealthy families want to trade land with the Park Service so they can build up to 15 private homes, some up to 15,000 sq ft, inside wilderness Congress said in 1972 must stay "permanently preserved in its primitive state."

It's loggerhead sea turtle nesting ground, home to 30% of Georgia's total, plus four other protected sea turtle species, red knots, and piping plovers. A watchdog group had to FOIA the draft deed terms just to see them. Georgia's own Camden County Commission wouldn't endorse the deal.

A former Yosemite superintendent called that deal "so ridiculous, it makes you sick."

Here's the mechanism. The Land and Water Conservation Fund exists specifically to buy and protect public land, funded by offshore oil and gas royalties, as an environmental offset for that drilling. Burgum's Interior has been trying to redirect that same money away from buying conservation land and toward "deferred maintenance" instead. Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-NM) says that diversion is illegal and expects it to get sued over.

So the fund meant to protect land from exactly this kind of loss is being hollowed out, then tapped again to help pay private developers to take park land in the first place.

This isn't one bad deal. It's a pattern. How many other national parks does this admin have waiting in the pipeline, ready to be sliced off to private interests?

Tell NPS this shouldn't move forward funded by conservation dollars it was never meant to touch. We don't have much time. Link is in the first reply.
